docs.title: ENUMs Usage Reference — MT4Account
docs.text: Which low-level MT4Account methods take or return protobuf enums, and how you pass them in Ruby.

docs.title: 💎 How enums work in Ruby
docs.text:
In the Ruby protobuf runtime, an enum value is a Ruby symbol — both when you pass it in and when you read it back. There are no module constants to import (unlike Python/Node): you write the value's name as a :SYMBOL.

# IN — a sort selector enum, passed as a symbol:
orders = mt4.account.opened_orders(sort: :SORT_BY_OPEN_TIME_ASC)   # EnumOpenedOrderSortType
bars   = mt4.account.bars("EURUSD", timeframe: :M5, from_utc: Time.now.to_i - 86_400)  # mapped to QHB_PERIOD_M5

# OUT — an enum-typed field reads back as a symbol:
acc = mt4.account.account_summary
acc.account_trade_mode        # => :ACCOUNT_TRADE_MODE_DEMO   (EnumAccountTradeMode)
mt4.account.opened_orders.first&.order_type   # => :OO_OP_BUY   (OpenedOrderType)

Don't know a value's exact spelling? List any enum with the Protobuf Inspector:

ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb enum OpenedOrderType
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb whereenum OrderSendOperationType

Mind the context — order type lives in different enums per call. When you send an order the field is OrderSendOperationType (OC_OP_*); when you read the open book or history it's OpenedOrderType (OO_OP_*); in streams it's SUB_ORDER_OPERATION_TYPE (SUB_OP_*). Same six directions, three different names.

docs.title: ✅ Summary
docs.text:
Method Group With enums Total % Account & Stats 2 6 33% Orders & History 2 3 67% Symbols & Quotes 3 9 33% Trading Operations 2 4 50% Streaming Methods 2 5 40% Total 11 27 41%

Plus the connection helper connect_proxy, which takes a ProxyTypes enum (4): :None, :Https, :Socks4, :Socks5.

docs.title: 👤 1. Account & Stats — 2/6 use enums
docs.text:
Method In / Out Input enum Output enum account_summary 0 / 2 — EnumAccountTradeMode (3): :ACCOUNT_TRADE_MODE_DEMO/_CONTEST/_REAL · EnumAccountMarginMode (3): :ACCOUNT_MARGIN_MODE_RETAIL_NETTING/_EXCHANGE/_RETAIL_HEDGING server_timezone 0 / 1 — SERVER_TIMEZONE_SOURCE (3): :SERVER_TIMEZONE_SOURCE_UNKNOWN/_LIVE/_LAST_VALIDATED trade_stats · trade_stats_equity_history · equity_history · trade_unrealized_pl 0 / 0 — — (plain numeric stats)

MT4 has no account_info_double/integer/string (those are MT5) — read account values straight off account_summary.

docs.title: 📋 2. Orders & History — 2/3 use enums
docs.text:
Method In / Out Input enum Output enum opened_orders 1 / 1 EnumOpenedOrderSortType (4): :SORT_BY_OPEN_TIME_ASC/_DESC, :SORT_BY_ORDER_TICKET_ID_ASC/_DESC OpenedOrderType (8) on order_type orders_history 1 / 1 EnumOrderHistorySortType (6): :HISTORY_SORT_BY_OPEN_TIME_*, :_CLOSE_TIME_*, :_ORDER_TICKET_ID_* OpenedOrderType (8) on order_type opened_orders_tickets 0 / 0 — —

OpenedOrderType (8): :OO_OP_BUY (0), :OO_OP_SELL (1) (market = positions) · :OO_OP_BUYLIMIT (2), :OO_OP_SELLLIMIT (3), :OO_OP_BUYSTOP (4), :OO_OP_SELLSTOP (5) (pending) · :OO_OP_BALANCE (6), :OO_OP_CREDIT (7) (ledger).

docs.title: 📊 3. Symbols & Quotes — 3/9 use enums
docs.text:
Method In / Out Input enum Output enum symbols · symbol_select · quote · quote_many · tick_value_with_size 0 / 0 — — symbol_params_many 0 / 3 — in SymbolParamsManyInfo: SP_ENUM_SYMBOL_TRADE_MODE (5) on TradeMode, SP_ENUM_SYMBOL_TRADE_EXECUTION (4) on TradeExeMode, SP_ENUM_TRADE_CALC_MODE (3) on TradeCalcMode bars 1 / 0 QUOTE_HISTORY_TIMEFRAME (:QHB_PERIOD_M1 … :QHB_PERIOD_MN1, value = minutes) — quote_history 1 / 0 ENUM_QUOTE_HISTORY_TIMEFRAME (:QH_PERIOD_M1 … :QH_PERIOD_MN1, ordinals 0–8) —

You pass the friendly :M1 … :MN1 to bars / quote_history; the SDK maps it to the right timeframe enum. The two timeframe enums differ (modern QHB_PERIOD_* vs legacy QH_PERIOD_*).

docs.title: 💰 4. Trading Operations — 2/4 use enums
docs.text:
Method In / Out Input enum Output enum order_send 1 / 0 OrderSendOperationType (6): :OC_OP_BUY/_SELL/_BUYLIMIT/_SELLLIMIT/_BUYSTOP/_SELLSTOP — order_modify 0 / 0 — — order_close (order_close_delete) 0 / 1 — OrderCloseDeleteMode (2): :OCD_MARKET_ORDER, :OCD_PENDING_ORDER order_close_by 0 / 0 — —

The MT4Service / MT4Sugar trade helpers accept a friendly type: (:buy, :sell_limit, …) and map it to OrderSendOperationType (:OC_OP_*) for you — you only reach for the raw enum at the MT4Account level. The raw protobuf field rejects :buy; it needs :OC_OP_BUY.

docs.title: 📡 5. Streaming Methods — 2/5 use enums
docs.text: Method In / Out Output enums on_symbol_tick · on_opened_orders_tickets · on_connect_state 0 / 0 — on_opened_orders_profit 0 / 2 MT4_SUB_ENUM_EVENT_GROUP_TYPE (2): :OrderProfit, :OrderUpdate on type · SUB_ORDER_OPERATION_TYPE (6): :SUB_OP_BUY … on each order's type on_trade 0 / 2 MT4_SUB_ENUM_EVENT_GROUP_TYPE (2) on type · SUB_ORDER_OPERATION_TYPE (6) on the order rows inside event_data

docs.title: ⚠️ Special cases
docs.text:
1. No MT5-style property selectors. MT4 has no *_info_double/integer/string methods, so there are no *PropertyType input enums — you read fields directly off the result messages.
  2. No "deals" enums. MT4 has orders, not positions/deals, so there is no deal-type / deal-entry enum family (those are MT5).
  3. Three order-type enums by context. OrderSendOperationType (OC_OP_*, sending) · OpenedOrderType (OO_OP_*, reading) · SUB_ORDER_OPERATION_TYPE (SUB_OP_*, streaming). The friendly :buy/:sell/... only works on the Service/Sugar trade helpers.
  4. mql_code is not an enum field on the trade result. A rejection raises ApiError; the numeric e.mql_code has its symbolic names in the MqlErrorCode enum. See Return Codes.

docs.title: Getting Started with RubyMT4
docs.text: Quick setup — connect to MetaTrader 4 from Ruby in a few minutes.

docs.title: What is RubyMT4?
docs.text:
RubyMT4 is a Ruby client for MetaTrader 4 accounts over the MetaRPC gRPC API (mt4.mrpc.pro:443). It's organised in three layers you can mix freely:

  • MT4Account — raw gRPC, protobuf in/out, full control.
  • MT4Service — typed Ruby Structs, plain arguments.
  • MT4Sugar — one-line helpers.

See the Project Map for how they fit together. (MetaRPC::MT4::Client aliases MT4Sugar; MetaRPC::MT4::Account aliases MT4Account.)

MT4 has orders, not positions. An open market order IS the position, and there is no trade retcode — a filled order returns OrderSendData with a ticket > 0. Keep this in mind throughout; see MT4 for Beginners.

docs.title: Install & downloads
docs.text: Two ways to use RubyMT4 — take our ready-made project, or take only the protocol and build your own client.

docs.title: 1 · Take our project (recommended)
docs.text:
The complete thing we built: the three layers (MT4Sugar / MT4Service / MT4Account), the error/stream helpers, and the generated stubs — all wired together as the metarpc_mt4 gem.

  • Just the library, for your own app — the gem isn't on RubyGems, so point Bundler at the repo:
# Gemfile
gem "metarpc_mt4", git: "https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyMT4.git"

bundle install

Then require "metarpc_mt4". Brings the SDK and the protobuf stubs (under the gem's package/).

  • The full repo (adds the runnable examples/demos/ and the tests):
git clone https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyMT4.git
cd RubyMT4
bundle install
ruby examples/demos/main.rb 6     # run a demo (6 = sugar basics)

🎓 New here? Start with the full repo (the git clone above). You get all three layers side by side (MT4Account → MT4Service → MT4Sugar) and ready-made examples written on each of them that you can run and read. Learn the SDK this way first — only once you're comfortable should you consider building your own from the raw protos (option 2 below).

🪟 Windows note. The grpc gem ships prebuilt binaries for Windows (x64-mingw-ucrt) only through 1.84.1 — newer versions are source-only and need a full build toolchain. On Windows, pin it in your Gemfile: gem "grpc", "~> 1.84.1". (The repo's Gemfile already does this.)

docs.title: 2 · Take only the protos and build it yourself (raw gRPC)
docs.text:
For advanced use — after you know the SDK. Skip our layers and talk to the gateway from the generated stubs directly. The stubs ship in the package/ folder (mt4-term-api-*_pb.rb, *_services_pb.rb, and mrpc-mt4-error_pb.rb).

Download just the package/ folder (not the whole repo) — any of these:

# A) quickest — grab only the subfolder (no git history)
npx degit MetaRPC/RubyMT4/package package

# B) pure git — sparse-checkout only package/
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --no-checkout https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyMT4.git
cd RubyMT4 && git sparse-checkout set --no-cone 'package/**' && git checkout

# C) via Bundler — then copy the folder out of the installed gem
bundle install          # with the Gemfile git source above
cp -r "$(bundle show metarpc_mt4)/package" ./package

Then install the gRPC + protobuf runtime next to it:

gem install grpc -v 1.84.1 google-protobuf googleapis-common-protos-types

Put package/ on the load path and require the service stubs:

$LOAD_PATH.unshift(File.expand_path("package", __dir__))
require "mt4-term-api-market-info_services_pb"   # etc.

The raw .proto sources (to regenerate stubs for another language or version) are on the MT4 Client API Explorer → Download MT4 Protos.

⚠️ The stubs are not standalone — take the whole package/ folder, not single files. Each *_pb.rb cross-requires its siblings (e.g. mrpc-mt4-error_pb) by bare name, so package/ must be on $LOAD_PATH. This path gives you raw gRPC with no 3-layer SDK — see the Protobuf Inspector.

docs.title: 🔑 API Key & Authentication
docs.text:
Connecting to the MetaRPC production endpoint (mt4.mrpc.pro:443) uses a personal API key — you get one just by registering on our site:

  1. Sign up — create a free account at https://mrpc.pro/signup.
  2. Copy your key — it's provisioned automatically; open the MT4 Client API Explorer and your key is shown at the top (Active · Copy key). Nothing to generate.
  3. Use it — pass the key to MT4Sugar.create(host, port, api_key:) (or set the MRPC_API_KEY environment variable instead of hard-coding it).

You'll also need an MT4 demo account (login / password / server, e.g. EGlobal-Demo) — see MT4 for Beginners to create one (one click for $1, or free via the MT4 terminal).

💡 TRIAL / keyless. No account yet? Pass the literal value "TRIAL" as the key to connect for a first look. Your own key — free from sign-up — is for normal use.

docs.title: 🆔 Session ID is automatic
docs.text: You never call get_id or supply an id header. On connect / connect_ex the server generates a terminal session GUID (terminal_instance_guid) and the SDK attaches it — alongside your API key — to every later request and stream automatically. Prefer passing a stable id: per strategy so the gateway reuses one terminal.

docs.title: Connect & read the account
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt4"

mt4 = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Sugar.create("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt4.connect(1235959737, "password", server: "EGlobal-Demo")

a = mt4.account_info
puts "##{a.login} — #{a.balance} #{a.currency} · 1:#{a.leverage}"

Prefer environment variables? Set MT4_LOGIN / MT4_PASSWORD / MT4_SERVER and read them into mt4.quick_connect(login, password, server).

docs.title: A first trade (demo)
docs.text:
r = mt4.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)          # tiny demo order
puts r.ticket.positive? ? "opened ##{r.ticket} @ #{r.price}" : "not filled"

o = mt4.open_orders(symbol: "EURUSD").max_by(&:ticket)
mt4.close_order(o.ticket) if o

MT4 has no retcode: a filled order returns OrderSendData with a ticket > 0. A rejection raises MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError — read e.mql_code (130 invalid stops, 132 market closed, 134 not enough money, 138 requote). A transport failure after the request may have reached the terminal raises a TradeOutcomeUnknown-marked error — don't blindly retry. See Return Codes & the error model.

docs.title: Dropping down a layer
docs.text:
Need something the sugar layer doesn't expose? Go down:

service = mt4.service   # MT4Service — typed Structs
account = mt4.account   # MT4Account — raw protobuf

q    = service.quote("EURUSD")    # Quote(bid, ask, high, low, spread, time_utc)
tick = account.quote("EURUSD")    # raw Mt4TermApi::QuoteData

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The MT4, trading and SDK terms you'll meet in these docs, grouped by kind.

docs.title: 🏗️ Architectural terms
docs.text:
Three-layer architecture — the SDK is three decoupled layers, each owning the one below (sugar.service → MT4Service, service.account → MT4Account). See the Project Map.

MT4Account — the low-level layer. Raw gRPC: you pass protobuf *Request messages and read *Reply / *Data replies via their snake_case accessors. Owns the channel, the gRPC stubs, auth metadata, reconnect and streaming. → overview

MT4Service — the mid layer. Same calls, but it builds the protobuf from plain arguments and returns typed Ruby Structs (Account, Quote, SymbolSpec). → overview

MT4Sugar — the high layer. One-line helpers (buy_market, close_all) with smart defaults; trade helpers return the result data (a filled order has ticket > 0). → overview

Struct (DTO) — the plain Ruby Struct objects MT4Service returns instead of protobuf (Account, Quote, SymbolSpec), with read-only attribute methods.

ApiError — the error raised when the gateway or terminal reports a problem (MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError). InvalidLoginError flags never-retry auth failures; TradeOutcomeUnknown marks a trade whose result is uncertain after a transport failure. See Return Codes → the error model.

Subscription — what a streaming method returns (MetaRPC::MT4::Subscription): call cancel to stop the stream; count / error report its state.

Client / Account aliases — MetaRPC::MT4::Client aliases MT4Sugar; MetaRPC::MT4::Account aliases MT4Account.

docs.title: 💎 Ruby-specific concepts
docs.text:
Blocks for streams — a streaming method yields each payload to the block you pass, and returns a Subscription to stop it.

sub = mt4.on_symbol_tick("EURUSD") { |t| puts "#{t.bid} / #{t.ask}" }
# later:
sub.cancel

Keyword arguments — optional parameters are passed by name, not position.

mt4.connect(1235959737, "password", server: "EGlobal-Demo")
mt4.buy_market_with_sl_tp("EURUSD", 0.01, sl: 1.0820, tp: 1.0920, comment: "demo")

Enums as symbols — protobuf enums are Ruby symbols, both in and out (:ACCOUNT_TRADE_MODE_DEMO, :OO_OP_BUY, :OC_OP_BUY). See the ENUMs Reference.

o = mt4.open_orders.first
o.order_type           # => :OO_OP_BUY   (a symbol)

Typed Structs vs protobuf stubs — the low layer returns generated protobuf objects (snake_case accessors like o.order_type, o.profit); the mid/high layers unwrap or filter them for you. Discover real field names with the Protobuf Inspector.

d  = mt4.account.opened_orders   # low: [OpenedOrderInfo] protobuf (market + pending)
ps = mt4.service.positions       # mid: only the market orders (positions), filtered

Error handling — begin / rescue — wrap calls that can fail; rescue MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError (or its subclasses).

begin
  mt4.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError => e
  warn "trade failed: #{e.code} (mql #{e.mql_code})"
end

Connection & cleanup — connect / quick_connect opens the terminal session; disconnect closes it and (with delete: true) frees the terminal (a trial allows one per IP). Use ensure.

begin
  # …
ensure
  mt4.disconnect
end

docs.title: Account
docs.text: Balance — closed-trade money; excludes floating P/L. Equity — balance + credit + floating P/L; moves with open orders. Margin — funds locked to hold orders. Free margin — equity − margin; available to open more. Margin level — equity / margin × 100 (%); low levels risk a stop-out. Leverage — the multiplier (1:100) setting margin need. Trade mode — DEMO, CONTEST or REAL.

docs.title: Instruments & prices
docs.text: Symbol — a tradable instrument (EURUSD, XAUUSD). Bid / Ask — sell / buy price; spread = ask − bid. Digits — decimal places (5 for EURUSD, 3 for JPY). Tick — one price update (quote / on_symbol_tick). MT4 quotes carry bid/ask/high/low (no last).

docs.title: Orders (the MT4 model)
docs.text:
MT4 has orders, not positions. An open market order IS the position — there is no separate position object, and no "deals" list.

Order — an instruction to trade. Market fills now (:buy / :sell); pending (:buy_limit / :sell_limit / :buy_stop / :sell_stop) waits for a price. Ticket — the numeric id you modify / close; order_send returns it (ticket > 0 = filled). Order type — two enums by context: OrderSendOperationType OC_OP_* (when sending), and OpenedOrderType OO_OP_* (when reading the open book; OO_OP_BUY/SELL are market = positions, the ...LIMIT/STOP are pending, OO_OP_BALANCE/CREDIT are ledger rows). SL / TP — stop-loss / take-profit auto-close levels. Magic number — a client id tagging a strategy's orders. No retcode — unlike MT5, MT4 has no returned_code; a rejection raises ApiError with an mql_code. See Return Codes.

docs.title: 📦 Technical concepts
docs.text:
Point — the smallest price increment (0.00001 on 5-digit EURUSD). Pip — the conventional move unit; on a 3- or 5-digit symbol pip = point × 10, so one pip on EURUSD = 0.0001. Tick value / tick size — the money value of one tick, and the price change one tick represents — inputs for P&L and sizing (tick_value_with_size).

Lot / volume — trade size in lots (0.01 = micro). Must obey volume limits (volume_min / volume_max / volume_step). Contract size — units of the base instrument per 1.0 lot.

Risk-based sizing — picking the lot so a stop of N pips loses a fixed amount. MT4 has no server-side calc RPC, so the SDK estimates locally: pip_value, required_margin and max_lot. Risk amount = balance × risk_percent / 100. Required margin — margin a prospective order needs (leverage-based estimate). Drawdown — the drop from a peak to current equity, %.

Stops level (TradeStopsLevel) — minimum distance, in points, SL/TP may sit from the market; closer → mql_code 130 (invalid stops).

Trailing stop — a stop that ratchets in your favour, never back (orchestrator). Breakeven — moving the stop to entry once in profit. Hedging — holding BUY and SELL on one symbol at once. Grid trading — bracketing price with pending orders (orchestrator). Scalping — many small short-lived trades. Kill-switch — close everything on a drawdown/margin breach (risk manager).

docs.title: 🔌 gRPC & protocol terms
docs.text:
gRPC — the RPC protocol the SDK speaks to mt4.mrpc.pro:443 (HTTP/2 + protobuf over TLS).

Protobuf — the binary message format. On the low layer you build *Request messages and read *Reply replies via snake_case accessors; MT4Service hides this behind typed Structs. The generated stubs live in package/.

Streaming pattern — a server stream delivered via a block: a streaming method yields each payload and returns a Subscription. See gRPC Stream Management.

Gateway — the MetaRPC service (mt4.mrpc.pro) bridging the SDK to MT4 terminals and managing sessions. Terminal — the MT4 instance your account runs on behind the gateway. Session / terminal instance guid — the id obtained on connect (ConnectEx), attached with your API key to every later call automatically (on mt4.account.server_guid). API key — your MetaRPC key; pass it to MT4Sugar.create(...), or use "TRIAL".

docs.title: gRPC Streaming & Subscription Management
docs.text:
How real-time server streams work in RubyMT4 — subscribe with a block, stop cleanly with cancel, and never leak a reader thread.

This guide covers:

  • ✅ How to subscribe to market-data and trade-event streams
  • ✅ How to stop a stream without leaking its background thread
  • ✅ Patterns from a 5-second snapshot to a managed background service
  • ✅ The model behind every stream (one thread + a Subscription)
  • ✅ Error handling and best practices

docs.title: The model in one picture
docs.text:
Every streaming method takes a block and immediately returns a MetaRPC::MT4::Subscription. The actual reading happens on a background thread the SDK spawns for you — your block is called once per message as it arrives, while your main code keeps running.

your block  ◄──yields each message──  background Thread  ◄──gRPC server stream──  mt4.mrpc.pro:443
     ▲                                        │
     └──────────  sub.cancel  stops the thread (and joins it, up to 5 s)

There is no polling and no async/await — Ruby threads do the work. A Subscription is the handle you keep to stop it (cancel), wait on it (join), check it (alive?, count, error). This is the whole lifecycle; master cancel and you're done.

No auto-reconnect. If the stream drops, the reader thread ends and sub.error is set — the SDK does not resubscribe for you. Re-open it yourself if you need resilience.

docs.title: Quick Start — the simplest subscription
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt4"

mt4 = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Sugar.create("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt4.quick_connect(1235959737, "password", "EGlobal-Demo")

# on_symbol_tick / subscribe_ticks yields each tick to the block, returns a Subscription
sub = mt4.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") do |t|
  puts "#{t.symbol}  bid #{t.bid}  ask #{t.ask}"
end

sleep 5        # let it stream for 5 seconds while the main thread does other work
sub.cancel     # stop cleanly — cancels the stream and joins the reader thread
puts "received #{sub.count} ticks"

When to use: quick examples, testing, short monitoring sessions.

subscribe_ticks (sugar/service) and on_symbol_tick (account) are the same stream — the sugar name just reads better. The block receives a tick (symbol, bid, ask, last, volume, time, time_utc), not a wrapper. (MT4 ticks carry bid/ask — last is usually 0 on FX.)

docs.title: Available streaming methods
docs.text:
All of these take a block and return a Subscription. They exist on MT4Account (raw) and are re-exposed by MT4Service / MT4Sugar under friendlier names.

Method (Account) Sugar / Service name Yields What it streams on_symbol_tick(symbols) subscribe_ticks(symbols) a tick real-time bid/ask per symbol on_trade on_trade OnTradeData orders opened / modified / closed on_opened_orders_profit(interval_ms:) on_opened_orders_profit(...) OnOpenedOrdersProfitData open orders' P/L, every interval_ms on_opened_orders_tickets(interval_ms:) on_tickets(interval_ms:) tickets snapshot open position & pending-order tickets on_connect_state(terminal_ids) on_connect_state(...) ConnectStateData the terminal's connect-state changes

Plus a blocking convenience that streams ticks for a fixed time and returns the count (no Subscription to manage):

n = mt4.each_tick("EURUSD", seconds: 5) { |t| puts t.bid }   # blocks 5 s, then returns n

Reference: Streaming Methods overview · MT4Sugar → Streaming. Run it: ruby examples/demos/main.rb 3 (raw) · ruby examples/demos/main.rb 5 (service).

docs.title: Pattern 1 — Time-boxed snapshot
docs.text:
The blocking each_tick is the shortest path when you just want N seconds of data:

count = mt4.each_tick(["EURUSD", "GBPUSD"], seconds: 10) do |t|
  puts "#{t.symbol}: #{t.bid}"
end
puts "#{count} ticks in 10s"

docs.title: Pattern 2 — Count-limited (stop after N messages)
docs.text:
Keep the Subscription and cancel it from inside the block once you've seen enough:

sub = nil
seen = 0
sub = mt4.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") do |t|
  seen += 1
  puts "[#{seen}] #{t.bid}"
  Thread.new { sub.cancel } if seen >= 50   # cancel off the reader thread
end
sub.join        # wait for it to finish

Why Thread.new { sub.cancel }? cancel joins the reader thread, so calling it from that same thread would deadlock. Cancel from the main thread (Pattern 3) or hand it off to a short-lived thread as above.

docs.title: Pattern 3 — Condition-based stop (from the main thread)
docs.text:
Signal with a flag; the main thread does the cancel:

target_hit = false
sub = mt4.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| target_hit = true if t.bid > 1.10000 }

sleep 0.1 until target_hit || !sub.alive?
sub.cancel
puts target_hit ? "target reached after #{sub.count} ticks" : "stream ended early"

docs.title: Pattern 4 — Background service with guaranteed cleanup
docs.text:
Wrap the lifetime in begin/ensure so the stream is always stopped, even on error or Ctrl-C:

sub = mt4.on_opened_orders_profit(interval_ms: 1000) do |data|
  data.opened_orders_with_profit_updated.sort_by { |o| -o.order_profit }.first(5).each do |o|
    puts "#{o.symbol}  #{o.order_profit.round(2)}"
  end
end

begin
  sleep 30            # run the service for 30 s (or loop your own logic here)
ensure
  sub.cancel          # ALWAYS stop it
end

docs.title: Multiple concurrent streams
docs.text:
Each subscription is independent (its own thread), so just open several and cancel them all. Collect the handles so cleanup is one loop:

subs = []
subs << mt4.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| puts "[TICK] #{t.bid}" }
subs << mt4.on_trade              { |_e| puts "[TRADE] event" }
subs << mt4.on_opened_orders_profit(interval_ms: 2000) { |d| puts "[P/L] #{d.opened_orders_with_profit_updated.size} orders" }

begin
  sleep 30
ensure
  subs.each(&:cancel)   # stop every stream
end

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
A stream's reader thread swallows the expected GRPC::Cancelled on cancel. Any other error is stored on the subscription as sub.error (it does not raise in your main thread), and the thread ends — so a stream can stop on its own:

sub = mt4.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| handle(t) }
sleep 10
sub.cancel

if sub.error
  warn "stream failed: #{sub.error.class}: #{sub.error.message}"   # e.g. a MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError
end

Check sub.alive? to see whether a stream is still running, and sub.count for how many messages it has delivered. A per-message error reported by the server (a *Reply with an error) is raised inside the thread as MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError and lands in sub.error. See Return Codes & the error model.

docs.title: ✅ DO
docs.text:
1. Always keep the Subscription a streaming method returns — it's your only handle to stop it.
  2. Always cancel when done (wrap long-lived streams in begin/ensure).
  3. Cancel from the main thread (or a throwaway thread), never from inside the reader block — cancel joins the thread.
  4. Prefer each_tick for simple time-boxed sampling — it manages the subscription for you.
  5. Check sub.error after a stream you expected to keep running has stopped — there is no auto-reconnect.
  6. Collect handles (subs << …) when running several streams, so cleanup is one each(&:cancel).

docs.title: ❌ DON'T
docs.text:
1. Don't drop the handle (mt4.subscribe_ticks(...) { } with no sub =) — you can never stop that thread.
  2. Don't call sub.cancel inside its own block — it deadlocks (join-on-self). Signal a flag or spawn a thread.
  3. Don't forget ensure — an exception in your loop would otherwise leave the reader thread running.
  4. Don't assume a stream is alive — the server or network can end it; re-check alive? / error and resubscribe if needed.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Streaming Methods overview — every stream, with its payload fields
  • OnSymbolTick · OnTrade — per-method references
  • MT4Sugar → Streaming — the friendly subscribe_ticks / each_tick helpers
  • Glossary → Subscription · Return Codes & errors

Remember: one block, one background thread, one Subscription. Keep the handle, cancel in an ensure, and your streaming code stays leak-free. 🚀

docs.title: MT4 for Beginners
docs.text: New to MetaTrader 4? This is the 5-minute mental model you need before the code makes sense.

docs.title: What MT4 is
docs.text:
MetaTrader 4 (MT4) is a trading platform. Your account lives on a broker's server (e.g. EGlobal-Demo). Through it you trade symbols (instruments like EURUSD or XAUUSD).

This SDK talks to your MT4 terminal over the network (gRPC to mt4.mrpc.pro:443) so you can automate everything from Ruby.

Always learn on a demo account. It trades with fake money on real prices — no risk.

docs.title: Getting a demo account & API key
docs.text:
Registration and your API key are free. Sign up at mrpc.pro/signup and your key is provisioned automatically — nothing to generate; in the web Explorer it's even attached to every call for you. What costs money is paid usage of the service (for example the instant $1 demo below).

To run the SDK you also need an MT4 demo account (login / password / server). You can get one two ways:

docs.title: ⚡ Fastest — one click on mrpc.pro ($1)
docs.text:
Our MT4 Client API Explorer (a live API playground) spins up a demo account instantly — no terminal install:

  1. Open the MT4 Client API Explorer (sign in first). Your API key is already shown at the top (Active · Copy key).
  2. Click Open demo account ($1). The $1 is charged to your MetaRPC balance (the account that holds your API key) — not to a broker.
  3. The demo is created instantly with a ready login / password / server — you can even run real API calls right on that page (the key is attached automatically).

Copy the demo login / password / server, then jump to Getting Started to connect from Ruby.

docs.title: 🖥️ Free — create a demo in the MetaTrader 4 terminal
docs.text:
The no-cost route: create a demo account directly in the MT4 terminal (free), and connect with your free API key — or with the literal value "TRIAL" for a quick first look.

1 · Download & install MT4. Get the terminal from metatrader4.com/download and install it.

2 · Find the Navigator panel. It's on the left, below Market Watch. Its Accounts section is where you add accounts.

3 · Open a new account. Right-click Accounts → Open an account to bring up the broker-server search.

4 · Pick a demo server. Find your broker's demo server (search if needed) and click Next.

5 · Choose "Open a new demo account" and click Next.

6 · Fill in the form (name, email; virtual deposit e.g. $10,000, leverage 1:100, currency USD), accept the terms, Next.

7 · Save your credentials. MT4 shows your login, password (master) and server. Copy them now — the SDK needs exactly these three values.

Two passwords are shown: the master password trades; the investor password is read-only. Use the master password with the SDK.

docs.title: The money words
docs.text:
Term In one line Balance Your settled money (no open trades counted). Equity Balance plus the profit/loss of trades you have open right now. Margin Money "reserved" while a trade is open. Free margin What's left to open new trades.

When you open a trade, equity moves tick by tick. When you close it, the result folds into balance.

docs.title: Buying and selling
docs.text:
• Buy (go long) — you profit if the price rises.
  • Sell (go short) — you profit if the price falls.

You trade in lots (volume). 0.01 is a micro lot — the smallest typical size, perfect for learning.

Two ways to enter:

  • Market order — fill now at the current price.
  • Pending order — wait for a price. A LIMIT waits for a better price; a STOP waits for a breakout.

docs.title: Protecting a trade
docs.text:
• Stop-Loss (SL) — auto-close if the price goes against you by so much. Caps the loss.
  • Take-Profit (TP) — auto-close once you've made your target.

Set them as prices — compute the distances from pips (pip = point × 10 on a 5-digit symbol):

pip    = mt4.symbol_point("EURUSD") * 10
digits = mt4.symbol_digits("EURUSD")
q      = mt4.price("EURUSD")

# 20-pip stop, 40-pip target
mt4.buy_market_with_sl_tp("EURUSD", 0.01,
  sl: (q.bid - 20 * pip).round(digits),
  tp: (q.ask + 40 * pip).round(digits))

See Risk Management for sizing a trade to a fixed risk.

docs.title: MT4's model: orders are positions
docs.text:
This is the one thing to remember — and it's where MT4 differs from MT5:

  • An order is the instruction to trade.
  • On MT4, a filled market order IS the open trade (the "position"). There is no separate position object, and no "deals".
  • Each order has a ticket — the number you use to modify or close it.

So "close the position" means close the order by its ticket. There is also no trade retcode: a filled buy_market returns OrderSendData with a ticket > 0; a rejection raises an error.

docs.title: Your first 10 lines
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt4"

mt4 = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Sugar.create("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt4.quick_connect(login, "password", "EGlobal-Demo")

puts "balance #{mt4.balance.round(2)}"
r = mt4.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)          # tiny demo trade
mt4.close_order(r.ticket)                     # r.ticket is the order (= position) ticket

docs.title: 🧱 The three layers
docs.text:
RubyMT4 is built in three decoupled layers. Your code can enter at any level, and each layer owns the one beneath it (sugar.service → the MT4Service, service.account → the MT4Account). MetaRPC::MT4::Client aliases MT4Sugar; Account aliases MT4Account.

Layer Source What it does Overview 3 · MT4Sugar lib/metarpc_mt4/mt4_sugar.rb One-line helpers: buy_market, close_all, risk sizing, SL/TP. 11 groups. MT4Sugar overview 2 · MT4Service lib/metarpc_mt4/mt4_service.rb Typed facade: plain args in, typed Ruby Structs out (Account, Quote, SymbolSpec). No protobuf. 5 groups. MT4Service overview 1 · MT4Account lib/metarpc_mt4/mt4_account.rb Low-level gRPC: protobuf request/reply, connect/session, streaming. Everything builds on it. 5 groups. MT4Account overview

docs.title: 🎮 Running the demos

The demos (laid out in the tree above) run from one menu — pass a number to run one directly:

docs.title: 🎯 Which layer should you use?
docs.text:
• Most trading apps → MT4Sugar. One-liners, risk-based sizing and SL/TP keep your code short and safe.
  • Custom execution → MT4Service. Typed calls when you manage your own flow.
  • Protocol-level control → MT4Account. Raw protobuf requests and streams.
  • New to MT4? → MT4 for Beginners, then Getting Started.
  • Mirror trades to other accounts? → SDK Ecosystem → Trade Copier.

docs.title: Protobuf Inspector — Interactive Type Explorer
docs.text:
A small offline tool that reads the generated MT4 protobuf stubs and tells you the real field names, types and enum values — so you never guess an accessor again.

The generated stubs under package/*_pb.rb are the raw contract. When you need to know "what's the exact accessor on this reply?" or "what are the valid values of this enum?", the inspector answers from the descriptors themselves — no connection, no API key, no trades.

Source: examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb

docs.title: 🏁 Running it
docs.text:
It's a standalone helper (it does not go through the demo menu, which connects first):

# interactive REPL
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb

# one-shot — pass a command as arguments, get the answer, exit
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb OrderSendData
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb enum OrderSendOperationType
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb field order_type
ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb search Tick

The REPL opens on a summary of what it discovered:

================================================================
MT4 PROTOBUF INSPECTOR (Ruby)
================================================================
  219 message types · 26 enums discovered
  Type 'help' for commands, 'list' to browse, 'exit' to quit.

>

Offline & safe. It only requires the package/*_pb.rb message stubs and reads their descriptors. It never opens a channel. You can run it with no credentials at all.

docs.title: 🧰 Commands
docs.text:
Command What it shows Example list [--msg\|--enum] all message types and/or enums list --enum <TypeName> a message's fields (name · type · label · #) OpenedOrderInfo search <text> message and enum names containing <text> search Order field <name> which messages carry a field named <name> field order_type findtype <type> every field of a proto type, grouped by message findtype double enum <Name> an enum's values (sorted by number) enum OrderSendOperationType whereenum <Name> which message fields use an enum whereenum OpenedOrderType stats type / field / enum counts stats help or ? the command list help exit / quit / q leave the REPL exit

Name lookups are fuzzy: exact → case-insensitive exact → a single partial match → otherwise it lists the candidates.

docs.title: A message's fields — <TypeName>
docs.text:
Fields print as name · proto-type · label · field-number. Message/enum fields show their subtype inline (enum<…> / message<…>). This is how you catch the naming gotchas the stubs hide — e.g. SymbolTickValueWithSizeInfo uses PascalCase/camelCase accessors:

> SymbolTickValueWithSizeInfo

TYPE: SymbolTickValueWithSizeInfo   (5 fields)
================================================================
  index              int32                            (#1)
  symbolName         string                           (#2)   ← i.symbolName, not i.symbol_name
  TradeTickValue     double                           (#3)   ← i.TradeTickValue, not i.trade_tick_value
  TradeTickSize      double                           (#4)
  TradeContractSize  double                           (#5)

The field name is the accessor you call in Ruby.

🐛 A real MT4 spelling gotcha. The commission field is spelled commision (single "m") on OpenedOrderInfo / HistoryOrderInfo, but commission (double "s") on the streamed OnOpenedOrdersProfitOrderInfo. And the streamed row's profit is order_profit, not profit. One OnOpenedOrdersProfitOrderInfo lookup settles it.

docs.title: Which message has a field? — field <name>
docs.text:
> field order_type

FIELD 'order_type'
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
exact match in (2): HistoryOrderInfo, OpenedOrderInfo

So both the open book and history rows expose order_type — the kind of check this command ends in seconds.

docs.title: An enum's values — enum <Name>
docs.text:
> enum OrderSendOperationType

ENUM: OrderSendOperationType
================================================================
  OC_OP_BUY       = 0
  OC_OP_SELL      = 1
  OC_OP_BUYLIMIT  = 2
  OC_OP_SELLLIMIT = 3
  OC_OP_BUYSTOP   = 4
  OC_OP_SELLSTOP  = 5

docs.title: Where is an enum used? — whereenum <Name>
docs.text:
> whereenum OpenedOrderType

ENUM 'OpenedOrderType' used in (2 fields)
================================================================
  HistoryOrderInfo.order_type
  OpenedOrderInfo.order_type

docs.title: All fields of a type — findtype <type>
docs.text:
> findtype double

FIELDS OF TYPE 'double' (… in … messages)
================================================================
  AccountSummaryData: account_balance, account_equity, account_credit, account_margin, account_margin_free, account_margin_level
  QuoteData: bid, ask, high, low
  …

Valid type names are the proto scalar/compound types: double, float, string, bool, int32, int64, uint32, uint64, message, enum.

docs.title: Counts — stats
docs.text:
> stats
================================================================
  message types : 219
  message fields: 874
  enums         : 26
  enum values   : 252

docs.title: 🧭 The "three order_type enums" gotcha
docs.text:
search order reveals why a BUY constant that works in one call fails in another — the API has separate order-type enums per context:

Enum Use it for Values OrderSendOperationType order_send (opening/placing orders) OC_OP_* OpenedOrderType reading opened_orders / orders_history OO_OP_* SUB_ORDER_OPERATION_TYPE streaming events (on_trade, on_opened_orders_profit) SUB_OP_*

When a call rejects your enum, whereenum <Name> confirms whether that enum is even accepted by the message you're building. The friendly :buy/:sell/... only works on the Service/Sugar trade helpers — the raw order_send field needs :OC_OP_BUY. See ENUMs Reference.

docs.title: 📦 Common use cases
docs.text:
1. "undefined method on a reply." Run <ReplyType> and read the real field names — e.g. symbolName / TradeTickValue (camel/Pascal), commision (single "m").
  2. "What value do I pass for the order type?" enum OrderSendOperationType (and mind the context table above).
  3. "Which request/reply do I need?" search <keyword> lists both messages and enums matching the name.
  4. "Which messages even have this field?" field <name> — exact and partial hits with the real field spelling.
  5. "Where is this enum accepted?" whereenum <Name> before you build the request.

docs.title: ℹ️ How it works
docs.text:
Ruby's protobuf runtime exposes a descriptor on every generated type. The inspector walks the Mt4TermApi namespace, classifies each constant as a message (Google::Protobuf::Descriptor) or an enum (Google::Protobuf::EnumDescriptor), and reads fields (name, type, label, number, subtype) and enum pairs straight from those descriptors. That's why it's always in sync with the stubs — there's no hand-maintained list to drift.

Because Ruby descriptors carry field numbers, proto types, labels and subtypes, this inspector reports more than the raw getter/setter names you'd see in some other SDKs — you get the full field shape.

docs.text:
• MT4Account overview — the documented API over these stubs
  • ENUMs Reference — which enum belongs to which call
  • Return Codes & errors — the error model and mql_code
  • Getting Started → raw gRPC — taking only the package/ stubs

Tip: reach for the inspector the moment a field or enum name is in doubt — one field or enum lookup is faster than reading a stub by hand.

docs.title: Return Codes & the Error Model
docs.text: How RubyMT4 tells you a trade's result. MT4 has no retcode: a filled order returns OrderSendData with ticket > 0; a rejection raises ApiError carrying an MQL4 error code; and TradeOutcomeUnknown marks a trade whose fate is uncertain.

docs.title: 🛡️ MT4 has no returned_code
docs.text:
Unlike MT5, there is no returned_code field. A trading operation either:

  • succeeds → returns its *Data with a ticket > 0 (for order_send) or a success flag, or
  • is rejected → raises MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError, whose mql_code tells you why (130 invalid stops, 132 market closed, 134 not enough money, 138 requote…).
begin
  r = mt4.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)       # returns OrderSendData
  puts r.ticket.positive? ? "opened ##{r.ticket} @ #{r.price}" : "not filled"
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError => e
  puts "rejected: #{e.code} (mql #{e.mql_code} #{e.error.mql_error_code})"
end

Golden rule: a trade that raised did not fill; a trade that returned a ticket > 0 did. Read-only calls (prices, symbols, balance) also raise on failure and otherwise return data.

docs.title: 🧭 The three outcomes of a trade call
docs.text:
Outcome How it surfaces What it means Done returns OrderSendData, ticket > 0 the broker executed it Rejected raises MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError broker said no — reason in e.mql_code / e.error.mql_error_description Uncertain raises a TradeOutcomeUnknown-marked error (or an ApiError with trade_outcome_unknown?) request may or may not have executed — do not blindly retry

So a complete trade looks like:

begin
  r = mt4.buy_market_with_sl_tp("EURUSD", 0.01, sl: 1.0820, tp: 1.0920)
  puts r.ticket.positive? ? "opened ##{r.ticket} @ #{r.price}" : "not filled"
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::TradeOutcomeUnknown => e
  warn "UNCERTAIN — check open orders before retrying: #{e.message}"
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError => e
  warn "trade error: #{e.mql_code} #{e.error.mql_error_description}"
end

docs.title: 📥 What the trade data carries
docs.text:
Trade one-liners return the operation's *Data:

> OrderSendData              # ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb OrderSendData
  ticket        int32     ← > 0 means FILLED (the order = position id)
  volume        double
  price         double
  open_time     Timestamp
  open_time_utc Timestamp

OrderModifyData carries order_was_modified (bool); OrderCloseDeleteData carries mode (:OCD_MARKET_ORDER / :OCD_PENDING_ORDER). None of them carry a retcode — success is the ticket / flag, failure is an exception.

docs.title: ❗ The error object (MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError)
docs.text:
When the gateway answers with the error branch, the SDK raises MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError, wrapping the protobuf Error. Useful accessors:

On the error Gives e.message the full formatted string (code, type, MQL code + description) e.code the gateway error_code string (e.g. "MRPC_TIMEOUT", "API_KEY_INVALID", "CONNECT_EX_INVALID_LOGIN_ERROR") e.mql_code the numeric MQL4 error (e.g. 130) — alias for e.error.mql_error_int_code e.error.mql_error_code the same as an enum symbol (e.g. :ERR_INVALID_STOPS) e.error.mql_error_description human MQL4 error text e.error.type the gateway error class (:MRPC, :MRPC_TIMEOUT, :TERMINAL_API_TIMEOUT, :MQL_EXECUTION…) e.api_key_error? true for API_KEY_INVALID / API_KEY_REQUIRED — never retry e.trade_outcome_unknown? true when the trade's result is uncertain (see below)

Subclass InvalidLoginError < ApiError is raised by connect when the broker rejects the login — never retry it.

rescue MetaRPC::MT4::InvalidLoginError
  abort "bad login/password/server"
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError => e
  case e.mql_code
  when 134 then warn "not enough money — reduce volume"
  when 132 then warn "market closed — try during trading hours"
  when 130 then warn "stops too close — widen SL/TP (TradeStopsLevel)"
  when 138, 135 then warn "requote / price changed — resend with a fresh price"
  else warn "error #{e.code}: #{e.error.mql_error_description}"
  end
end

docs.title: ⚠️ TradeOutcomeUnknown — the one you must not retry blindly
docs.text:
A trade call can fail after the request may already have reached the terminal (a gateway/terminal timeout, or a transport drop like gRPC UNAVAILABLE / DEADLINE_EXCEEDED). The trade may or may not have executed. The SDK never re-sends a trade automatically.

Two ways it reaches you, both answering trade_outcome_unknown? == true:

begin
  r = mt4.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::TradeOutcomeUnknown => e   # transport failure, mixed into the GRPC error
  warn e.to_s
  # check whether it actually opened before doing anything:
  o = mt4.open_orders(symbol: "EURUSD").max_by(&:ticket)
  # decide to keep it or send again — never retry unconditionally
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError => e
  retry_safely unless e.trade_outcome_unknown?  # in-band timeout (mql 128, MRPC_TIMEOUT…)
end

In-band uncertainty is flagged for trade RPCs when the gateway code is a timeout (MRPC_TIMEOUT, TERMINAL_API_TIMEOUT, COMMAND_TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED, TERMINAL_API_CALL_TIMEOUT), the error type is :MRPC_TIMEOUT / :TERMINAL_API_TIMEOUT, or the MQL code is 128 (ERR_TRADE_TIMEOUT).

docs.title: 📋 MQL4 error codes (MqlErrorCode)
docs.text: MT4's mql_code is a standard MQL4 runtime/trade error (not an MT5 TRADE_RETCODE_*). These are the trade-relevant ones, exactly as the enum defines them in package/. List them all with ruby examples/demos/helpers/17_protobuf_inspector.rb enum MqlErrorCode.

docs.title: Server / connection — retry with a delay
docs.text: Code Name Meaning 4 ERR_SERVER_BUSY trade server busy 6 ERR_NO_CONNECTION no connection to the trade server 8 ERR_TOO_FREQUENT_REQUESTS too many requests 128 ERR_TRADE_TIMEOUT trade timed out — uncertain outcome 136 ERR_OFF_QUOTES no prices right now 137 ERR_BROKER_BUSY broker busy 141 ERR_TOO_MANY_REQUESTS too many requests 146 ERR_TRADE_CONTEXT_BUSY trade context busy

docs.title: Requote — resend with a fresh price
docs.text: Code Name 135 ERR_PRICE_CHANGED 138 ERR_REQUOTE

docs.title: Validation — fix the request
docs.text: Code Name Common cause 3 ERR_INVALID_TRADE_PARAMETERS malformed request 129 ERR_INVALID_PRICE price breaks symbol rules 130 ERR_INVALID_STOPS SL/TP too close (TradeStopsLevel) 131 ERR_INVALID_TRADE_VOLUME volume < min / > max / wrong step 145 ERR_TRADE_MODIFY_DENIED modification too close to market / frozen 147 ERR_TRADE_EXPIRATION_DENIED expiration not allowed by the broker

docs.title: Restrictions — check trading conditions
docs.text: Code Name 132 ERR_MARKET_CLOSED 133 ERR_TRADE_DISABLED 139 ERR_ORDER_LOCKED 140 ERR_LONG_POSITIONS_ONLY_ALLOWED 148 ERR_TRADE_TOO_MANY_ORDERS 149 ERR_TRADE_HEDGE_PROHIBITED 150 ERR_TRADE_PROHIBITED_BY_FIFO

docs.title: Money / account
docs.text:
Code Name 64 ERR_ACCOUNT_DISABLED 65 ERR_INVALID_ACCOUNT 134 ERR_NOT_ENOUGH_MONEY

The enum also defines the full MQL4 runtime range (4000+, e.g. ERR_WRONG_FUNCTION_POINTER) — those are MQL program errors, not trade rejections, and rarely surface through the API.

docs.title: 🔁 A retry pattern
docs.text:
MT4 raises on rejection, so categorise by mql_code and let trade_outcome_unknown? gate the uncertain ones:

REQUOTE   = [135, 138].freeze
TEMPORARY = [4, 6, 8, 136, 137, 141, 146].freeze

def buy_with_retry(mt4, symbol, volume, tries: 3)
  tries.times do |i|
    begin
      r = mt4.buy_market(symbol, volume)
      return r if r.ticket.positive?
    rescue MetaRPC::MT4::TradeOutcomeUnknown
      raise                               # never auto-retry an uncertain trade
    rescue MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError => e
      raise e if e.trade_outcome_unknown?
      code = e.mql_code
      raise e unless REQUOTE.include?(code) || TEMPORARY.include?(code)  # permanent → stop
      sleep(REQUOTE.include?(code) ? 0.1 : i + 1)                        # requote fast, temp backoff
    end
  end
  nil
end

docs.title: 📑 Quick category reference
docs.text: Category MQL4 codes Action Success (no code — ticket > 0) continue Requote 135, 138 resend immediately with a fresh price Temporary 4, 6, 8, 136, 137, 141, 146 retry with a delay Uncertain 128 (+ MRPC_TIMEOUT / transport drop) check open orders, don't blind-retry Validation 3, 129, 130, 131, 145, 147 fix the request Restrictions 132, 133, 139, 140, 148, 149, 150 check conditions Money / account 64, 65, 134 reduce volume / check account

docs.title: The MetaRPC SDK family
docs.text:
Where RubyMT4 sits — and how it pairs with the Trade Copier to mirror a strategy across accounts.

MetaRPC ships two families of SDKs. They share the same authentication (an ApiKey sent as gRPC metadata plus an owner user_key in the body), the same gRPC-over-TLS transport to *.mrpc.pro, the same mrpc.pro portal and the same demo onboarding — but they do different jobs.

Family Job Endpoint SDKs Terminal SDKs operate one trading account — connect, read, trade, stream mt4.mrpc.pro:443 (MT4) RubyMT4, GoMT4, CSharpMT4, CppMT4, JavaMT4, PyMT4, NodeMT4 (+ MT5 variants) Copier SDKs mirror trades between accounts (master → followers) copy.mrpc.pro:443 RubyCopier, NodeCopier, GoCopier, CSharpCopier, PyCopier, …

RubyMT4 is a Terminal SDK. When you want to replicate what happens on one account to others, reach for the Copier SDK — in Ruby that's RubyCopier (metarpc_copier).

docs.title: How RubyMT4 and RubyCopier relate
docs.text:
RubyMT4 (this SDK) RubyCopier Scope one account a master → follower pair Does connect, quotes, buy_market, streams start · list · pause · remove a copier Endpoint mt4.mrpc.pro:443 copy.mrpc.pro:443 Thinks in ticks, orders (= positions on MT4) risk sizing, pause/resume, copy logs

One sentence: RubyMT4 is where trades are produced and observed on an account; RubyCopier is how they're distributed to followers.

docs.title: The bridge — a shared terminal session
docs.text:
A copier account carries an optional id — a terminal session GUID. That's exactly the value RubyMT4 obtains on connect: after connect / connect_ex, the session GUID (terminal_instance_guid) lives on mt4.account.server_guid. So an account you're already running with RubyMT4 can be enrolled into a copier without the copier reconnecting it — pass that GUID (hyphenated via RubyCopier.to_hyphen_guid) as the account id.

RubyCopier understands account type values MT4 (and MT5, cTrader CT, TradeLocker TL) — the same MRPC-hosted terminals RubyMT4 drives.

docs.title: End-to-end: run a strategy on the master, replicate to a follower
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt4"
require "rubycopier"      # git clone'd alongside; see Install below

KEY = ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"]   # owner key — note: TRIAL is NOT accepted by the copier

# 1 · Operate the MASTER account with RubyMT4
master = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Sugar.create("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: KEY)
master.quick_connect(ENV["MASTER_LOGIN"].to_i, ENV["MASTER_PASSWORD"], "EGlobal-Demo")
master_session_id = RubyCopier.to_hyphen_guid(master.account.server_guid)  # the ConnectEx GUID → copier id

# 2 · Start a copier: MASTER → FOLLOWER (RubyCopier, on copy.mrpc.pro)
copier = RubyCopier::CopierService.new("copy.mrpc.pro:443", user_key: KEY)
rep = copier.start(
  risk_type:  "LotMultiplier",   # or "FixedLot" + risk_value "0.1"
  risk_value: "1.0",
  copy_sl: true, copy_tp: true,
  master: { type: "MT4", user: ENV["MASTER_LOGIN"].to_i, password: ENV["MASTER_PASSWORD"],
            server: "EGlobal-Demo", id: master_session_id },
  slave:  { type: "MT4", user: ENV["SLAVE_LOGIN"].to_i,  password: ENV["SLAVE_PASSWORD"],
            server: "EGlobal-Demo" },
)
abort "copier start failed: #{rep.error}" unless rep.ok
puts "copier ##{rep.copier_id} running"

# 3 · Trades you now place on the master via RubyMT4 replicate to the follower
master.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
# … the copier mirrors the open (and the later close) onto the follower account

# 4 · Tidy up
copier.remove(rep.copier_id)

Install: RubyCopier isn't on RubyGems — clone it (git clone https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyCopier.git && cd RubyCopier && bundle install) and require its lib/rubycopier, or point a Gemfile at the repo: gem "metarpc_copier", git: "https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyCopier.git".

Risk sizing (the copier's risk_type): FixedLot · LotMultiplier · BalanceMultiplier · FixedBalanceMultiplier · EquityMultiplier. Plus copy_sl / copy_tp / copy_pending_orders / reverse_copy. Manage a running copier with copier.list, copier.pause(id, paused: true) and copier.remove(id).

docs.title: 🧩 Notes & gotchas
docs.text:
• Two services, two endpoints. RubyMT4 talks to mt4.mrpc.pro; RubyCopier to copy.mrpc.pro. The copier is a companion service, not a replacement.
  • Owner key required for the copier. TRIAL works for a first look on a terminal, but CopierService.new raises without a real owner user_key.
  • Transport success ≠ broker execution. A successful start means the copier was created — confirm the follower actually opened the trade (RubyCopier's logs, or read the follower with RubyMT4's open_orders).
  • Demo-first. Use disposable demo accounts for copier tests. Hosted terminals and running copiers are billed separately (see pricing).

docs.title: Synchronous Calls & Threaded Streaming
docs.text: How RubyMT4 actually executes: every request/response call is synchronous and blocking; the only concurrency is streaming on background threads. There is no async/await or Fiber API.

docs.title: 🎯 The model in one line
docs.text:
• Request/response calls (account info, quotes, trading, history) block the calling thread and return a value (or raise). Linear, simple, predictable.
  • Streaming calls (subscribe_ticks, on_trade, …) run on a background thread and invoke your block per message, returning a Subscription immediately — your main thread keeps going.
  • Want parallelism for blocking calls? Spawn your own Ruby Threads. The gRPC layer releases the GVL while waiting on the network, so independent calls can be in flight at once.
Blocking call Background-thread stream Returns the result value a Subscription (immediately) Blocks your thread? yes, until the reply no — the block runs on the reader thread Use for everything request/response live ticks, trade & P/L events Stop it n/a (it already returned) sub.cancel

docs.title: ✅ Synchronous calls (the default — everything)
docs.text:
Just call and use the result. No await, no runtime to set up:

require "metarpc_mt4"

mt4 = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Sugar.create("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt4.connect(1235959737, "password", server: "EGlobal-Demo")

a = mt4.account_info          # blocks, returns an Account Struct
q = mt4.price("EURUSD")       # blocks, returns a Quote
r = mt4.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)   # blocks, returns OrderSendData (ticket > 0 = filled)
puts "balance #{a.balance}  bid #{q.bid}  ticket #{r.ticket}"

This is the right model for CLI scripts, one-off tasks, notebooks, and the demos — read top to bottom.

docs.title: 🧵 Concurrency with your own threads
docs.text:
Because each call blocks only its own thread, you parallelise by spawning threads. Independent reads then wait concurrently instead of one-after-another:

# Quote several symbols at once
symbols = %w[EURUSD GBPUSD USDJPY XAUUSD]
quotes  = symbols.map { |s| Thread.new { [s, mt4.price(s)] } }.map(&:value).to_h
quotes.each { |s, q| puts "#{s}  #{q.bid} / #{q.ask}" }

Share carefully. One connected mt4 multiplexes fine for reads over gRPC. For heavy concurrent trading, prefer a separate connection per worker (pass a stable id: per strategy) so sessions don't interleave. Guard any shared mutable state you build yourself with a Mutex. (A one-call batch like quotes — the sugar name for quote_many — is often simpler than threads for quotes.)

docs.title: 📡 Streaming is the built-in concurrency
docs.text:
A streaming method hands the work to a background thread and returns a Subscription. Your main thread is free while the block runs per message:

sub = mt4.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| puts "#{t.bid} / #{t.ask}" }
# ... main thread keeps working ...
sleep 5
sub.cancel          # stop cleanly (joins the reader thread)

Need a blocking sample instead? each_tick runs the stream inline for a fixed time and returns the count:

n = mt4.each_tick("EURUSD", seconds: 5) { |t| puts t.bid }

Full lifecycle, patterns and pitfalls (including don't cancel from inside the block): gRPC Stream Management.

docs.title: 💡 Rules of thumb
docs.text:
1. Default to straight synchronous code. It's the whole request/response API and it's the simplest thing that works.
  2. Use streaming for live data — it's already concurrent (a background thread), so you don't manage threads yourself.
  3. Add threads only when you have independent blocking work (e.g. many symbols) and the wall-clock saving matters — otherwise a batch call like quotes is simpler.
  4. Background jobs (a cron task, a Sidekiq/Resque worker) run this synchronous code as-is — nothing special required.
  5. There is no async/await here. If you see await in an example, it's from another language's SDK — the Ruby API is MT4Sugar.create(...) + connect.

docs.title: UserCode Sandbox
docs.text: Your blank canvas inside the demo suite — sugar arrives already connected, so you write only the trading logic.

docs.title: 🏁 Quick start
docs.text:
1. Open examples/demos/usercode/18_usercode.rb.
  2. Write your code inside the registered block (below the write your code below marker).
  3. Run it:
ruby examples/demos/main.rb 18

That's it — the menu connects once, then hands your block a live, connected sugar.

The sandbox as it ships:

Demos.register("18", "Sandbox - your own code (edit 18_usercode.rb)") do |sugar, cfg|
  sym = cfg.test_symbol

  # ─── write your code below ───
  puts "  balance #{format('%.2f', sugar.balance)}   #{sym} bid #{sugar.bid(sym)}"

  #   q    = sugar.service.quote(sym)
  #   tick = sugar.account.quote(sym)
  #   sugar.buy_market(sym, cfg.test_volume)   # ⚠ trades on a demo account
end

Keep it read-only while experimenting, or use tiny volumes on a demo account.

docs.title: 🎁 What's already set up
docs.text:
The block receives two arguments:

Argument What it is sugar a connected MT4Sugar — the high-level one-liners cfg the loaded config: cfg.test_symbol, cfg.test_volume, cfg.user, cfg.server, …

And from sugar you can reach every layer:

sugar            # MT4Sugar  — one-liners
sugar.service    # MT4Service — typed Structs (Quote, Account, SymbolSpec)
sugar.account    # MT4Account — raw gRPC / protobuf

No connect call, no API key handling — the launcher did it. Config comes from examples/demos/config/config.json or the MT4_LOGIN / MT4_PASSWORD / MT4_SERVER / MT4_SYMBOL / MT4_VOLUME env vars.

docs.title: 🧩 Mixing the three layers
docs.text:
All three are live at once — drop down whenever the sugar layer doesn't expose what you need:

# High — MT4Sugar
bal = sugar.balance                       # => Float

# Mid — MT4Service (typed Struct)
q = sugar.service.quote("EURUSD")         # Quote(bid, ask, high, low, spread, time_utc)

# Low — MT4Account (raw protobuf)
tick = sugar.account.quote("EURUSD")      # raw Mt4TermApi::QuoteData

docs.title: 📘 Quick reference (MT4Sugar)
docs.text:
# ── Account ──────────────────────────────────────────────
sugar.balance            # Float
sugar.equity             # balance + credit + floating P/L
sugar.free_margin        # available to open more
sugar.margin_level       # %
sugar.account_info       # Struct(login, balance, currency, leverage, …)
sugar.demo?              # true on a demo account

# ── Prices ───────────────────────────────────────────────
sugar.bid("EURUSD")      # Float
sugar.ask("EURUSD")
sugar.spread("EURUSD")
sugar.price("EURUSD")    # Quote(bid, ask, high, low, spread, time_utc)

# ── Market orders (return OrderSendData — ticket > 0 = filled) ──
r = sugar.buy_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
r = sugar.sell_market("EURUSD", 0.01)
r = sugar.buy_market_with_sl_tp("EURUSD", 0.01, sl: 1.0820, tp: 1.0920)

# ── Pending orders ───────────────────────────────────────
sugar.buy_limit("EURUSD", 0.01, 1.0850)
sugar.sell_stop("EURUSD", 0.01, 1.0750)

# ── Orders (MT4: a market order IS the position) ─────────
sugar.open_orders(symbol: "EURUSD")      # Array
sugar.count_orders
sugar.total_profit
sugar.has_order?("EURUSD")
sugar.close_order(ticket)
sugar.close_all
sugar.close_all_by_symbol("EURUSD")
sugar.cancel_order(ticket)               # delete a pending
sugar.modify_sl_tp(ticket, stop_loss: 1.0830, take_profit: 1.0930)

# ── History & stats (need from_utc:) ─────────────────────
sugar.order_history(from_utc: Time.now.utc - 24 * 3600)
sugar.trade_stats(from_utc: Time.now.utc - 7 * 86_400)

# ── Symbols & risk sizing (local estimates — no server calc) ──
sugar.symbol_digits("EURUSD")
sugar.symbol_point("EURUSD")
sugar.min_stop_level("EURUSD")
sugar.pip_value("EURUSD")                                # money per pip per lot
sugar.required_margin("EURUSD", 0.10, sugar.ask("EURUSD"))
sugar.max_lot("EURUSD", sugar.ask("EURUSD"))

# ── Streaming (block + Subscription) ─────────────────────
sub = sugar.subscribe_ticks("EURUSD") { |t| puts t.bid }   # sub.cancel to stop
n   = sugar.each_tick("EURUSD", seconds: 5) { |t| puts t.bid }  # blocking

Full lists: MT4Sugar · MT4Service · MT4Account.

docs.title: ✅ Checking a trade
docs.text:
MT4 has no retcode: a filled order returns OrderSendData with a ticket > 0; a rejection raises MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError:

begin
  r = sugar.buy_market(sym, cfg.test_volume)
  puts r.ticket.positive? ? "opened ##{r.ticket} @ #{r.price}" : "not filled"
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::TradeOutcomeUnknown => e
  warn "uncertain — check open orders before retrying: #{e.message}"
rescue MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError => e
  warn "trade error: #{e.mql_code} #{e.error.mql_error_description}"
end

See Return Codes & the error model for the full picture.

docs.title: 📝 A complete sandbox example
docs.text:
Risk-size a trade to ~1% of balance, open it, then report:

Demos.register("18", "Sandbox - your own code") do |sugar, cfg|
  sym = cfg.test_symbol
  q   = sugar.price(sym)
  pip = sugar.symbol_point(sym) * 10
  dig = sugar.symbol_digits(sym)

  sl  = (q.bid - 20 * pip).round(dig)                     # 20-pip stop
  tp  = (q.ask + 40 * pip).round(dig)

  # pip_value = money per pip per lot (a LOCAL estimate — MT4 has no calc RPC)
  lots = [((sugar.balance * 0.01) / (sugar.pip_value(sym) * 20)).round(2), 0.01].max

  if sugar.required_margin(sym, lots, q.ask) > sugar.free_margin
    puts "  not enough free margin for #{lots} lots"
  else
    r = sugar.buy_market_with_sl_tp(sym, lots, sl: sl, tp: tp)
    puts r.ticket.positive? ? "  opened ##{r.ticket} (#{lots} lots)" : "  not filled"
  end

  puts "  open: #{sugar.count_orders}  floating P/L: #{sugar.total_profit.round(2)}"
end

docs.title: 💡 Tips & common mistakes
docs.text:
1. Start read-only. sugar.balance, sugar.price(sym), sugar.open_orders can't hurt anything — learn the shapes first.
  2. Trade on demo, tiny volumes. Use cfg.test_volume (0.01) and confirm sugar.demo? before trading.
  3. Success is the ticket. A filled buy_market returns ticket > 0; a rejection raises (there is no retcode). Wrap trades in begin/rescue.
  4. Don't re-raise an uncertain trade blindly. On trade_outcome_unknown?, check open_orders first — the SDK never auto-resends a trade.
  5. Enum values are symbols (:OO_OP_BUY, :OC_OP_BUY), not constants — see ENUMs Reference.
  6. Unsure of a field or enum name? Ask the Protobuf Inspector.

docs.title: Your First Project
docs.text: Build a small, complete RubyMT4 script: connect, quote, trade with risk sizing, and report.

docs.title: 1 · Set up
docs.text:
mkdir mt4-bot && cd mt4-bot

Point Bundler at the repo (the gem isn't on RubyGems), then install:

# Gemfile
source "https://rubygems.org"
gem "metarpc_mt4", git: "https://github.com/MetaRPC/RubyMT4.git"
gem "grpc", "~> 1.84.1" if Gem.win_platform?   # Windows: prebuilt binary

bundle install

Create bot.rb. (Prefer the ready-made examples? git clone the repo and read examples/demos/ — see Getting Started.)

docs.title: 2 · Connect
docs.text:
require "metarpc_mt4"

mt4 = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Sugar.create("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])
mt4.quick_connect(
  ENV["MT4_LOGIN"].to_i,
  ENV["MT4_PASSWORD"],
  ENV["MT4_SERVER"],          # e.g. EGlobal-Demo
)
puts "connected? #{mt4.connected?}"

Need the MRPC_API_KEY? Register at https://mrpc.pro/signup — your key is provisioned automatically and shown in the MT4 Client API Explorer (Copy key). See Getting Started → API Key. (Or pass "TRIAL" for keyless access while testing.)

docs.title: 3 · Look at the market
docs.text:
symbol = "EURUSD"
q = mt4.price(symbol)
pips = (q.spread / mt4.symbol_point(symbol) / 10).round(1)
puts "#{symbol}  bid #{q.bid}  ask #{q.ask}  #{pips} pips"

docs.title: 4 · Trade with risk sizing
docs.text:
digits = mt4.symbol_digits(symbol)
pip    = mt4.symbol_point(symbol) * 10          # 1 pip on a 5-digit symbol
sl     = (q.bid - 20 * pip).round(digits)       # 20-pip stop
tp     = (q.ask + 40 * pip).round(digits)       # 40-pip target

# Size so the 20-pip stop risks ~1% of balance.
# pip_value = money per pip per 1.0 lot (a LOCAL estimate — MT4 has no server-side calc RPC).
pv   = mt4.pip_value(symbol)
lots = [((mt4.balance * 0.01) / (pv * 20)).round(2), 0.01].max

# Can we afford the margin? (required_margin is also a local leverage-based estimate)
if mt4.required_margin(symbol, lots, q.ask) > mt4.free_margin
  abort "not enough free margin for #{lots} lots"
end

r = mt4.buy_market_with_sl_tp(symbol, lots, sl: sl, tp: tp, comment: "first-project")
puts r.ticket.positive? ? "opened ##{r.ticket} with #{lots} lots" : "not filled"

MT4 has no retcode. A filled order returns OrderSendData with ticket > 0; a rejection raises MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError (read e.mql_code). Wrap the trade in begin/rescue in real code.

docs.title: 5 · Manage & report
docs.text:
puts "open orders: #{mt4.count_orders}"
puts "floating P/L: #{mt4.total_profit.round(2)}"

# tidy up for the demo
mt4.close_all

# today's realized result (MT4: closed orders — there is no separate "deals" list)
from   = Time.now.utc - 24 * 3600
closed = mt4.order_history(from_utc: from).reject { |o| %i[OO_OP_BALANCE OO_OP_CREDIT].include?(o.order_type) }
puts "today: #{closed.size} closed orders, net #{closed.sum(&:profit).round(2)}"

docs.title: 6 · Run it
docs.text:
MT4_LOGIN=1235959737 MT4_PASSWORD=secret MT4_SERVER=EGlobal-Demo \
MRPC_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY bundle exec ruby bot.rb

docs.title: MT4Account — Master Overview
docs.text:
One page to orient fast: what lives where, how to choose the right API, and jump links to every overview and method spec in this docs set.

MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Account (from the metarpc_mt4 gem) is the low-level layer — a thin, 1:1-with-the-wire client. Each method maps to a single gRPC RPC: you pass the plain arguments, it builds the generated protobuf *Request, sends it with the APIKey + terminal-id metadata, and returns the reply's *Data payload — or raises MetaRPC::MT4::ApiError. It owns the gRPC channel, the service stubs, the auth metadata and the connection lifecycle.

It exposes 26 feature methods across 5 groups (plus the connection helpers in Constructor & connection below). Defined in lib/metarpc_mt4/mt4_account.rb.

require "metarpc_mt4"
acct = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Account.new("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])

When to use this layer

Use MT4Account when you need a field the friendly layers do not expose, or full control over the exact request. For everyday work prefer MT4Service (plain args + typed Structs) or MT4Sugar (one-liners).

docs.title: 🚦 Start here — Section Overviews
docs.text:
• 1. Account Information Account snapshot (balance / equity / margin / leverage) and trading statistics — aggregate stats, equity curve, unrealized-P/L extrema.

  • 2. Orders & History Open orders (market + pending), their tickets, and closed-order history.

  • 3. Symbols & Quotes Symbols, Market Watch, live quotes, full specs, tick value, OHLC bars and the server time zone.

  • 4. Trading Operations Send, modify, close and close-by — the four order RPCs.

  • 5. Streaming Methods Real-time streams: ticks, trade events, orders-profit, ticket snapshots, connect-state.

docs.title: 🧭 How to pick a method
docs.text: If you need… Group Typical methods Account snapshot Account Information account_summary Performance stats / equity curve Account Information trade_stats, equity_history, trade_unrealized_pl Open orders / tickets / history Orders & History opened_orders, opened_orders_tickets, orders_history Live quotes / symbol specs Symbols & Quotes quote, quote_many, symbol_params_many, symbol_select OHLC bars / server time zone Symbols & Quotes bars, quote_history, server_timezone Place / modify / close an order Trading Operations order_send, order_modify, order_close_delete, order_close_by Real-time updates Streaming Methods on_symbol_tick, on_trade, on_connect_state

docs.title: 🔌 Usage pattern (raw gRPC)
docs.text:
Every method is called on an MT4Account. It owns the gRPC channel, sends the terminal id and API key as metadata, and unwraps the reply — returning the protobuf *Data payload or raising an error.

require "metarpc_mt4"

# Create the client (prepares the gRPC channel; api_key from MRPC_API_KEY)
acct = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Account.new("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"])

# Connect the terminal (ConnectEx by broker server name).
# The gateway returns a terminal session GUID; later calls reuse it automatically.
acct.connect(1235959737, "password", server: "EGlobal-Demo")

# Call a method: returns the *Data payload, or raises ApiError / a gRPC error.
s = acct.account_summary
puts "Balance: #{s.account_balance} #{s.account_currency}"

Every method follows the same shape:

  • Proto Service/Method: Service.Method(Request) → Reply
  • Client call: acct.method(args) returns the *Data payload.
  • Reply structure: the reply carries either a data payload or an error; MT4Account returns the data and turns error into a raised ApiError.
  • Errors are exceptions — there are no error return values; wrap calls in begin/rescue.

Field access: the generated protobuf messages expose snake_case readers — s.account_balance, not getAccountBalance(). A few symbol-spec messages use PascalCase accessors (p.Digits, p.VolumeMin); the friendly MT4Service layer normalizes these into plain Ruby Structs for you.

Timestamps: proto uses google.protobuf.Timestamp (read .seconds) on some messages and raw unix seconds on others (bars). MT4Service returns numbers / UTC instead.

Streaming methods: return a Subscription handle. The SDK reads the stream on a background thread and invokes your block for each payload; call subscription.cancel to stop.

docs.title: 🔐 Constructor & connection
docs.text:
The connection helpers are not separate method pages — they are the session plumbing every other call builds on. Create the client, then connect:

acct = MetaRPC::MT4::MT4Account.new("mt4.mrpc.pro", 443, api_key: ENV["MRPC_API_KEY"], id: stable_uuid)

# Connect by broker server (cluster) name — ConnectEx:
acct.connect(1235959737, "password", server: "EGlobal-Demo", name: "my-bot")
Helper What it does connect(login, password, server:, name:, …) Connect by broker server name (ConnectEx). Aliases: connect_ex, connect_by_server_name. Raises InvalidLoginError on bad credentials. connect_by_host(login, password, host:, port:, …) Connect by the broker trade server's raw host:port (Connect). connect_proxy(login, password, host:, port:, proxy_host:, proxy_port:, proxy_type:, …) Connect through a SOCKS/HTTP proxy. get_id(login, password) Resolve the terminal session id without connecting (GetId). check_connect / connect_state / connection_status Health checks — is the terminal still attached / its current state. reconnect(force:) Re-establish the broker connection with the stored parameters. disconnect(delete:, reason:) Stop the terminal (delete: true removes it from the account list). accounts(include_stopped:, page_size:) List the terminals owned by this API key (auto-paged). close Release the local gRPC channels (does not stop the terminal on the gateway).

connect_proxy enum — ProxyTypes (4): :None (0) · :Https (1) · :Socks4 (2) · :Socks5 (3). Pass one as proxy_type:.

Pass a stable id: per strategy so re-runs reuse one terminal instead of orphaning a new one. The gateway returns a session GUID on connect; the SDK attaches it (+ your api key) to every later call and stream automatically — you never pass it yourself. See Getting Started.
